title: Investment appraisal
overview: Investment appraisal compares long-term projects using payback, Accounting Rate of Return (ARR) and Net Present Value (NPV). You must calculate each method, understand what it measures, compare its strengths/limitations and integrate qualitative strategic factors before recommending a project.
syllabusPoints: Explain why businesses use investment appraisal.
Calculate and interpret NPV using discounted cash flow.
Use qualitative and quantitative factors to make investment decisions and compare method limitations.

definitions.definition: Time required for cumulative net cash inflows to recover the initial investment.
Average annual accounting profit as a percentage of average investment.
Factor converting a future cash flow into present value.
Total present value of future net cash flows minus the initial investment.
The principle that money available now is worth more than the same nominal amount received later.

sections.title: Why appraise investments
content: Major capital projects tie up finance for years and involve uncertain future returns. Appraisal provides structured evidence on liquidity, return and value, helping compare alternatives and justify resource allocation.

sections.title: Payback
content: Add net cash inflows until initial cost is recovered. Short payback is useful when liquidity/risk/technology change matter, but ignores cash flows after payback and usually ignores time value of money.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: If £100k is invested and £80k has been recovered after year 2, with £40k in year 3, another £20k/£40k=0.5 year -> payback 2.5 years.

sections.title: ARR
content: Uses average annual accounting profit and average investment, producing a familiar percentage. It considers profitability over the project life but uses accounting profit rather than cash and ignores timing of returns.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: ARR = Average annual profit / Average investment x100

sections.title: NPV
content: Discount each future net cash flow at the required rate and subtract the initial cost. Positive NPV means discounted inflows exceed the initial investment at that required return. Higher NPV generally adds more financial value, but forecasts and discount rate may be wrong.

examples.label: Worked example
examples.content: NPV = sum of discounted net cash inflows - initial investment

sections.title: Qualitative factors
content: Strategic fit, brand, employee impact, environmental effect, technological flexibility, legal constraints, risk and competitor reaction can outweigh a small numerical advantage. Quantitative appraisal supports judgement rather than replacing it.

sections.title: Comparing methods
content: Payback emphasises speed/liquidity, ARR accounting profitability and NPV timing/opportunity cost. Rankings can differ. Strong evaluation asks which criterion matters most for the business's objectives/risk and how reliable the forecasts are.

formulas.label: ARR
formulas.note: Use the definition required by the question if a different denominator is specified.

formulas.label: NPV
formulas.expression: sum of discounted net cash flows − initial investment
formulas.note: A positive NPV is financially acceptable at the chosen discount rate.

analysisChains.title: Positive net present value
steps: Discounted cash inflows exceed the initial cost
The project earns more than the chosen discount rate
Shareholder value should increase if forecasts are accurate
analysisChains.evaluation: NPV is only as reliable as its cash-flow forecasts and discount rate; strategic fit, risk and capacity constraints still matter.

examTips: Use cash flows for payback/NPV; use accounting PROFIT for ARR.
For partial-year payback, calculate the fraction of the final year.
Positive NPV is only as reliable as the cash-flow forecasts and discount rate.
commonMistakes: Using sales revenue rather than net cash flow in payback.
Automatically choosing shortest payback despite poor NPV/fit.
Forgetting the initial investment in NPV.
